steps.body: From a sequence, find a_1 and d, then use a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d. For 4, 7, 10, 13, … : a_1 = 4 and d = 3, so the 6th term is 4 + (6 − 1)·3 = 4 + 15 = 19.
Set the difference once and let position 6 read out.

widget.prompt: Dial the common difference so the 6th term of 4, 7, 10, 13, … lands on 19.
widget.successFeedback: d = 3: five gaps from the first term — 4 + 5·3 = 19. Position in, term out.
widget.lowFeedback: Too small — the 6th term falls short of 19. Check one gap: 7 − 4.
widget.highFeedback: Too big — the 6th term overshoots 19. The gaps in 4, 7, 10, 13 are smaller.

predict.reveal: a₆ = 4 + 5·3 = 19 in a single move — set d once and any position reads out directly. Step-by-step also works, but it doesn't scale to term 600; the formula does.

steps.body: You can also find **how far** a term is. In 5, 8, 11, … to reach 23: set 23 = 5 + (n − 1)·3, so 18 = (n − 1)·3, giving n − 1 = 6 and n = 7. The value 23 is the 7th term.

widget.prompt: In the sequence 5, 8, 11, ..., which term equals 23? (give n)

commonErrors.feedback: n − 1 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6, so n = 7 (add 1 back for the position).
18 ÷ 3 = 6 steps from the first term, so it's the 7th term.

steps.body: The same rule handles any term of any arithmetic sequence. Whether you want the 9th term or the position of a value, a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d does the work — no listing required.
